title: Define and implement initial Block representation
body:
## Goal

Design and implement the minimal data structures required to represent a Nysor Block in C++.

## Context

Nysor is based around composable Blocks that can be connected into graphs and eventually compiled into an executable representation. The goal is to determine the smallest useful representation (inputs, outputs, metadata) without prematurely locking the engine into a large runtime framework.

## Tasks

- Identify the minimum information a Block needs (ports, types, unique identifiers).
- Define how inputs and outputs are represented in memory.
- Create a small C++ prototype showing how a block is declared and configured.
- Document key design decisions (e.g. stateless vs stateful blocks).

## Expected result

A minimal Block definition/prototype in C++ along with unit tests.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome.

title: Implement a minimal Block Graph prototype
body:
## Goal

Create a minimal graph data structure capable of storing Nysor Blocks and their connections.

## Context

Nysor uses graphs to represent relationships between composable Blocks. Before compilation or validation can occur, we need a simple, stable graph representation.

## Tasks

- Implement a Graph class that stores nodes (Blocks) and edges (connections).
- Support adding and removing Blocks.
- Support connecting outputs to inputs.
- Implement basic traversal methods (e.g. iterating over nodes).

## Expected result

A working Graph implementation in C++ that can represent a simple network (e.g., Input → Transform → Output).

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome.

title: Implement graph validation
body:
## Goal

Create a validation system that can detect invalid Nysor graphs before compilation/execution.

## Context

A graph should be validated before it reaches later stages of the pipeline. Validation should catch structural and type-level problems early and return useful diagnostics rather than generic failure codes.

## Tasks

- Check for connections referencing nonexistent nodes or ports.
- Detect missing required inputs.
- Implement cycle detection in the graph.
- Check for type mismatch between connected ports.

## Expected result

A validation pass that can inspect a Graph and return diagnostic messages describing any safety violations.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome.

title: Prototype Graph → IR conversion
body:
## Goal

Create a small prototype that converts a validated Nysor graph into an intermediate representation (IR).

## Context

One of Nysor's central ideas is separating the user-facing graph from the representation used for compilation and execution. The IR should provide a cleaner representation for later optimization and scheduling.

## Tasks

- Define a minimal IR representation (e.g. linear instruction list or data-flow representation).
- Define how Blocks and connections map to IR instructions.
- Implement conversion from a valid graph into the IR.
- Verify that dependencies are preserved in the IR.

## Expected result

A minimal working Graph → IR converter and documentation showing an example conversion.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome.

title: Prototype dependency-based scheduling
body:
## Goal

Create a prototype that determines a valid execution order for dependent Nysor nodes.

## Context

A Nysor graph describes relationships between operations, but the runtime eventually needs a sequential or parallel execution plan. The scheduler should resolve dependencies and produce a valid execution order.

## Tasks

- Analyze dependencies between nodes in the graph or IR.
- Implement a basic topological scheduling algorithm.
- Handle independent nodes correctly.
- Ensure deterministic ordering where possible.

## Expected result

A scheduler that accepts a dependency graph/IR and outputs a valid execution sequence.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome.

title: Investigate graph optimization opportunities
body:
## Goal

Investigate and draft a design for potential optimization passes on the Nysor graph or IR.

## Context

Separating the user-facing graph from execution allows us to perform optimization passes (such as constant folding, dead-code elimination, or block fusion) to improve performance before runtime execution.

## Tasks

- Research common compiler optimization techniques applicable to block graphs.
- Propose a design for constant folding (evaluating static values at compile time).
- Propose a design for dead-code elimination (removing unconnected/unused blocks).
- Document how block fusion (merging multiple blocks into one) could be represented.

## Expected result

A research/design document outlining the proposed optimization passes and their feasibility.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome. A conclusion that a particular optimization is not worth the overhead is a valid result.

title: Build a tiny 2D proof of concept
body:
## Goal

Create a tiny example demonstrating how Nysor's architecture can represent a simple 2D game pipeline.

## Context

Nysor is ultimately intended to support game development, so we need small practical examples that test whether the architecture is actually useful and identify any architectural friction early.

## Tasks

- Define the Blocks required for the example (e.g. Input, Movement, Transform, Render).
- Construct the corresponding graph.
- Demonstrate graph validation, scheduling, or IR generation.
- Document any friction encountered while building the example.

## Expected result

A runnable or inspectable minimal 2D engine example demonstrating Nysor's compositional model.

## Notes

This is an architectural experiment. Alternative approaches are welcome. The goal is NOT to create a complete game, but to expose useful architectural insights.
